# CTL AEO-500 — 500 Cited AEO Questions on Black Culture (CultureTechLens)

 > 500 answer-engine question units on Black culture — each with a primary question, a cited direct answer (31-55 words), a 5-question cluster, keywords, a Wikidata QID or an honest NONE marker, and a dated verification note (2026-11-04). Assembled from the verified KG333 (333) and FC300 (167) registries. Citation statuses are the dataset's evidence vocabulary: 321 rows rest on Wikipedia/Wikidata, 88 fictional characters carry franchise coverage only, and 11 rows are GAPs where CultureTechLens is the source of record and no external page exists.

## Sample questions (answers as published in the dataset, with citations in the data file)
- **Why did MLK say 'I Have a Dream'?** Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was a Baptist minister and civil rights leader who led America's nonviolent civil rights movement. He delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech at the 1963 March on Washington, helped win landmark civil rights laws, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.
- **Why didn't Rosa Parks give up her seat?** Rosa Parks (1913–2005) was a seamstress and civil rights activist in Montgomery, Alabama. On December 1, 1955, she refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger and was arrested. Her act sparked the 381-day Montgomery Bus Boycott, a turning point in the civil rights movement.
- **How did Harriet Tubman free enslaved people?** Harriet Tubman (c. 1822–1913) was born enslaved in Maryland, escaped to freedom, and risked her life returning about 13 times on the Underground Railroad to free roughly 70 enslaved people. She later served the Union Army in the Civil War as a scout, spy, and nurse.
- **How did Frederick Douglass learn to read?** Frederick Douglass (c. 1818–1895) escaped slavery and taught himself to read and write, skills enslavers tried to deny him. He became the most famous abolitionist speaker of his time and told his own story in his bestselling 1845 Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass.
- **What did Sojourner Truth fight for?** Sojourner Truth (1797–1883) was born enslaved in New York, escaped with her infant daughter, and won freedom for her son in court. She became a traveling preacher and speaker for abolition and women's rights, famous for her 1851 speech remembered as 'Ain't I a Woman?'
- **Who was the first Black President?** Barack Obama (born 1961) was the 44th President of the United States, serving from 2009 to 2017, and the first Black president in American history. His presidency passed the Affordable Care Act health law, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2009.
- **Who was the first Black Vice President?** Kamala Harris (born 1964) served as Vice President of the United States from 2021 to 2025 — the first woman, first Black American, and first South Asian American to hold the office. She had previously been a U.S. Senator and California's Attorney General.
- **Who was the first Black Supreme Court Justice?** Thurgood Marshall (1908–1993) was the first Black justice on the U.S. Supreme Court, serving from 1967 to 1991. Before that, as a lawyer for the NAACP, he argued Brown v. Board of Education, the 1954 case that ruled school segregation unconstitutional.
- **What is 'good trouble'?** John Lewis (1940–2020) was a civil rights leader who helped lead the 1965 Selma voting rights march, where he was beaten on 'Bloody Sunday,' and later served Georgia in Congress for over 30 years. He called principled protest 'good trouble, necessary trouble.'
- **Who was the first Black woman to run for President?** Shirley Chisholm (1924–2005) became the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Congress in 1968, representing Brooklyn, New York. In 1972 she ran for president — the first Black candidate to seek a major party's presidential nomination — under the slogan 'Unbought and Unbossed.'
- **Why did Malcolm X change his name?** Malcolm X (1925–1965) was a Black rights activist and minister who taught Black pride, self-reliance, and self-defense against racism. After leaving the Nation of Islam he broadened his message toward human rights; his Autobiography, published after his assassination, remains a classic.
- **Who helped found the NAACP?** W.E.B. Du Bois (1868–1963) was a sociologist, historian, and co-founder of the NAACP in 1909. He was the first Black American to earn a Ph.D. from Harvard, and his 1903 book The Souls of Black Folk is one of the most important works in American history.
- **How did Ida B. Wells use newspapers to fight injustice?** Ida B. Wells (1862–1931) was an investigative journalist who used newspapers and pamphlets to expose lynching in America when few dared to. She co-founded the NAACP, fought for women's voting rights, and ran much of her crusade from Chicago.
- **Who refused to move on a bus before Rosa Parks, at 15?** Claudette Colvin (born 1939) was 15 years old in Montgomery, Alabama, when, on March 2, 1955 — nine months before Rosa Parks — she refused to give up her bus seat and was arrested. She later became a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle, the case that ended bus segregation.
- **Who was the 6-year-old who integrated her school?** Ruby Bridges (born 1954) was 6 years old in 1960 when she became the first Black child to integrate an all-white elementary school in the South, in New Orleans. Federal marshals escorted her past angry crowds, and she spent the year as the only child in her classroom.

## The GAP class — questions only CTL answers (CTL is the source of record)
- **Whose sermons from Alfred Street Baptist go viral?** Howard-John Wesley (born 1972) is the senior pastor of Alfred Street Baptist Church in Alexandria, Virginia, one of America's historic Black Baptist churches. His sermons circulate widely on YouTube, making him one of the most watched preachers of the digital era.
- **Who is Dallas' social justice pastor at Friendship-West?** Frederick D. Haynes III (born 1960) has pastored Friendship-West Baptist Church in Dallas since 1983, growing it into a megachurch known for social justice preaching. His sermons regularly go viral, and he briefly ran for Congress in 2024.
- **Who runs the African Diaspora News Channel on YouTube?** Phillip Scott is a YouTube news host who founded the African Diaspora News Channel, which covers news about Black people in America, Africa, and around the world for a large online audience. He is a leading example of independent Black digital journalism.
- **Who is The Black Authority on YouTube?** Jason Black, known online as Professor BlackTruth, is a YouTube commentator who hosts The Black Authority, a long-running channel of news analysis and interviews from a Black empowerment perspective, and has authored books and produced films for his audience.
- **Who co-anchors Good Morning America's weekend edition?** Janai Norman is an ABC News journalist who co-anchors the weekend edition of Good Morning America and anchors on ABC News Live. Known for warm, family-centered segments on parenting and wellness, she is one of morning TV's rising Black anchors — with no Wikidata entity yet.
- **Who is the lawyer-commentator behind The Reecie Colbert Show on YouTube?** Reecie Colbert is a political commentator and strategist who hosts The Reecie Colbert Show on YouTube and SiriusXM, known for data-driven breakdowns of Black voter behavior and election maps. A former federal budget analyst, she is one of independent Black media's fastest-growing voices — with no Wikidata entity yet.
- **Who is the YouTube essayist F.D Signifier?** F.D Signifier, born Fiqh Daniels, is a YouTube video essayist whose long-form essays on Black masculinity, hip-hop, film, and media — made from his background as a sociology educator in Atlanta — draw millions of views. He has no Wikidata entity or Wikipedia page yet: a clear Knowledge Graph gap.
- **Who was the first Black American honored in the US Capitol's Statuary Hall?** The statue of educator and civil rights leader Mary McLeod Bethune, unveiled in the US Capitol's National Statuary Hall in July 2022 representing Florida, made her the first African American honored with a state statue in the collection — sculpted by Nilda Comas from Italian marble.
- **What is the Ark of Return at the United Nations?** The Ark of Return, unveiled at United Nations headquarters in New York in 2015, is the UN's permanent memorial to the victims of slavery and the transatlantic slave trade — a triangular marble monument by Haitian-American architect Rodney Leon, sited where the world's diplomats must pass it.
- **Where is Alison Saar's Harriet Tubman statue?** Swing Low, Alison Saar's 13-foot bronze of Harriet Tubman, dedicated in 2008 in Harlem, New York, depicts Tubman striding forward with the roots of slavery pulling at her skirt — the first statue of a Black woman in a New York City public space in decades of monument building.
- **Where does Nelson Mandela stand in London?** The bronze statue of Nelson Mandela in London's Parliament Square, unveiled in 2007 while Mandela still lived — he joked he had become 'a tourist attraction' — places the South African freedom leader among Britain's statesmen, facing the Parliament he once petitioned from prison.
